Connect the hollow metal object to the negative terminal of a DC supply so that it is the cathode. Place the anode inside its cavity and connect it to the positive terminal. A suitable plating solution must be able to enter the cavity and contact both the inner surface to be plated and the anode. Leave a gap between the anode and the object; direct contact would short the circuit.
In the common soluble-anode plating model, the anode can be made of the metal to be deposited. Metal ions gain electrons at the object's cathodic inner surface and are reduced and deposited, while the anode can dissolve to replenish metal ions. Some plating processes instead use an insoluble anode and obtain the required metal ions from the bath. In either case, the essential arrangement here is the object as the cathode with the anode inside its cavity.
Arranging the anode to suit the cavity's shape and maintaining suitable spacing can improve the distribution of the inner coating, but this arrangement alone does not guarantee a perfectly uniform coating for every shape. If only the inner surface is to be plated, exposed outer surfaces can be masked. The question provides no data from which to specify a voltage, spacing, or coating thickness.

In the usual ideal electrolysis model, equal masses of the same substance are deposited at the corresponding electrodes of the cells, so the amounts in moles are equal as well. This assumes the same deposition reaction and ionic valence in each cell, with all the transferred charge used for that reaction and no bypass, shortage of reactant, or competing reaction.
Cells in series carry the same current at each instant, so the same total charge passes through each cell during the same interval. Faraday's law gives $m=kQ$, where $m$ is the deposited mass, $k$ is the electrochemical equivalent for the reaction, and $Q$ is the transferred charge. For constant current, $Q=It$, giving $m=kIt$. The same electrolyte undergoing the same deposition reaction has the same electrochemical equivalent. The current and elapsed time are also the same, so the deposited masses are equal. If the current varies with time, the total charge through each cell is still the same and the conclusion is unchanged.
Different concentrations affect resistance, voltage drops across the cells, and mass transport, but do not make series cells carry different currents. In real electrolysis, unequal current efficiencies for the product being compared, insufficient supply from a dilute solution, or different competing reactions can make the actual deposits unequal. Equal current efficiencies still give equal deposits. The question supplies no such nonideal parameters from which to calculate a different set of actual masses, and the ideal result must not be presented as an unconditional law for every real electrolytic cell.

The average current in the external circuit is 5 amperes. In the usual steady-conduction model of the question, this is the current.
Positive and negative ions drift in opposite directions in the electric field. Negative charge crossing the section in the opposite direction contributes conventional current in the same direction as the positive charge, so the two contributions add. The 3 coulombs and 2 coulombs are the respective magnitudes of charge transported in 1 second; they must not be subtracted merely because the ions have opposite charge signs.
$$I=\frac{3\,\mathrm{C}+2\,\mathrm{C}}{1\,\mathrm{s}}=5\,\mathrm{A}.$$
In the usual electrolytic circuit without a bypass or continuing charge accumulation, charge conservation makes the external current equal to the total current inside the cell. If only the total charge over this second is known and constant current is not assumed, 5 amperes is the average over that second, not proof that every instantaneous current is exactly 5 amperes.

In an ordinary electrolyte solution, dissolution, solvent interactions, and thermal motion form or separate mobile positive and negative ions. An applied electric field is not a necessary condition for this dissociation. For an ionic crystal such as sodium chloride, the solvent separates ions already present in the crystal and brings them into solution; it is not a process in which an electron is removed from every neutral molecule. Some molecular weak electrolytes form ions by reacting with the solvent and establish an equilibrium with undissociated material. In an ordinary electrolyte solution, the main current carriers are positive and negative ions, and an external field causes the existing ions to drift.
Gas ionization usually occurs when a neutral atom or molecule receives enough ionizing energy to lose an electron, producing a positive ion and a free electron. Ionizing radiation, sufficiently energetic collisions, or high temperatures can supply this energy. Some gases can also form negative ions by electron attachment, so an ionized gas must not be said to contain no negative ions at all. Free electrons and ions can both contribute to current in a gas.
The essential differences are the carrier-formation mechanism and the principal carrier types: dissociation in solution usually involves dissolution and solvent participation that produce or separate positive and negative ions, whereas gas ionization involves the detachment of electrons from neutral particles and normally requires ionizing energy. Both processes conserve electric charge; neither creates net charge from nothing.
